notes.meaning: Luke opens by reminding Theophilus of his first book, the Gospel of Luke. That gospel recorded what Jesus began to do and teach during his earthly life. This new book shows that Jesus continues his work from heaven through the Holy Spirit and his followers.

Luke explains that his first book ended on the day Jesus was taken up into heaven. Before ascending, Jesus gave specific commandments to his chosen apostles through the Holy Spirit. His guidance gives us confidence that the church's mission was directed by God from the very start.

After his death, Jesus proved he was truly alive by appearing to his followers many times over forty days. He ate with them, talked with them, and showed them his wounds so they could have no doubt about his physical resurrection. During this time, he taught them about the kingdom of God, which is God's spiritual rule in people's hearts and in the world.

While meeting with the apostles, Jesus commanded them not to leave Jerusalem just yet. They were to wait for the gift the Father had promised, which Jesus had spoken to them about before his death. He wanted them to wait for God's power rather than trying to do kingdom work in their own strength.

Jesus reminded them that John baptized people with water, but they would soon be baptized with the Holy Spirit. To be baptized with the Spirit means being immersed in his cleansing, renewing power and presence. This promised gift would arrive in just a few days to equip them for service.

differ.view: Spirit baptism occurs at the moment of salvation, placing every believer into the body of Christ.
Spirit baptism is an empowering experience that happens after conversion, usually accompanied by speaking in tongues.

notes.meaning: The apostles asked Jesus if he was finally going to restore the earthly kingdom to Israel at that time. Like many Jews of their day, they hoped the Messiah would overthrow foreign rulers and make Israel an independent, powerful nation. Their question showed they still had much to learn about the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom.

differ.view: The disciples were mistaken to hope for a political Jewish kingdom instead of Christ's spiritual reign through the gospel.
The disciples were correct to expect a future earthly kingdom for Israel, and Jesus only corrected their timing.

notes.meaning: Jesus told his followers that it was not for them to know the exact dates or periods set by the Father's authority. God keeps the timetable of future history in his own hands. Instead of guessing about dates, believers are called to trust God's plan and focus on the duties he gives them today.

Jesus promised that the disciples would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That spiritual power would make them his witnesses, starting in Jerusalem, moving through Judea and Samaria, and going to the ends of the earth. This promise outlines how the gospel message would spread across the world in the rest of the book.

As the disciples watched, Jesus was taken up from the earth and a cloud hid him from their sight. He left in plain daylight so they would be certain he had returned to the Father in heaven. This event showed them that his physical appearances on earth were finished and that he now rules as King in heaven.

The disciples kept looking intently into the sky as Jesus went up. Suddenly, two angels appearing as men in bright white clothing stood right next to them. God sent these heavenly messengers to comfort the disciples and turn their attention to what lay ahead.

The angels asked the disciples why they were still standing there gazing into the sky. They promised that this same Jesus would come back one day in the exact same visible, personal way he had left. That glorious return gives Christians hope and urges them to live faithfully while they wait.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Until Christ returns visibly at the end of time, he governs his church through visible successors to the apostles.

notes.meaning: The disciples immediately obeyed Jesus and walked back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives. The distance was about a Sabbath day's journey, which was less than a mile and within the travel limits of Jewish tradition. Their prompt return showed their trust in their Lord even though he was no longer physically with them.

When they entered the city, they went upstairs to the room where they were staying. Luke names all eleven remaining apostles to show they were united and restored after their earlier fear and running away. This small band of faithful leaders formed the core of the earliest church.

The apostles gathered regularly for united and earnest prayer. They were joined by several faithful women, by Mary the mother of Jesus, and by Jesus' brothers, who now believed in him after his resurrection. Waiting on God in prayer helped prepare their hearts to receive the Holy Spirit.

During those days of waiting, Peter stood up to speak before a gathering of about one hundred and twenty believers. He stepped forward as their natural leader, showing that he had fully recovered from denying Christ. This gathering shows the entire early church taking part in an important decision together.

Peter explained that the Old Testament Scriptures had to be fulfilled regarding Judas. Long ago, the Holy Spirit spoke through King David about the person who would lead the mob to arrest Jesus. Knowing that God foresaw this betrayal helped the believers understand that God's plans had not failed.

Judas had been chosen as one of the original twelve apostles and shared fully in their work. His privileged position made his betrayal of the Lord even more tragic and wicked. It stands as a solemn warning that holding a place of spiritual leadership does not guarantee a faithful heart.

Luke adds an explanation of how Judas died. The reward money for his wickedness was used to buy a field, where Judas fell headlong and his body burst open. His awful end became a lasting sign of the shame and ruin that come from betraying the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early traditions say Judas survived hanging but became bloated and died later, offering an alternative way to reconcile the biblical accounts.

notes.meaning: Everyone living in Jerusalem heard the shocking news about Judas and the field bought with his blood money. The local people called it Akeldama, an Aramaic name meaning Field of Blood. The site stood as a public reminder of Judas's guilt and the price paid for Jesus' life.

Peter quoted two passages from the Book of Psalms to explain what had happened. One psalm spoke of an enemy's home being left deserted, and the other said that another person should take his position of leadership. These scriptures showed the disciples that replacing Judas was in line with God's word.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The term used for Judas's office refers to a bishopric, showing that apostolic leadership was intended to continue through successor bishops.

notes.meaning: Peter explained the requirements for choosing a new apostle to fill the empty place. The man had to be someone who had accompanied the group throughout the entire time the Lord Jesus lived among them. Faithful, personal experience with Jesus from the beginning was essential for this ministry.

The candidate needed to have followed Jesus from John's baptism up to the day Jesus ascended to heaven. His main duty would be to join the apostles as an official eyewitness of Jesus' resurrection. The resurrection was the central truth they were called to proclaim to the world.

differ.view: The office of apostle was strictly limited to firsthand witnesses of the risen Christ and ceased when that generation died.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: While the original Twelve required personal companionship with Christ, later apostles like Paul and Barnabas show the office could continue.

notes.meaning: The believers nominated two men who met all the requirements: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus, and Matthias. Both men were trusted disciples who had followed Jesus faithfully. Neither man campaigned for the office, but both were willing to serve if chosen.

Before making a choice, the entire group prayed to the Lord, who knows the hearts of all people. They asked him to reveal which of the two men he had chosen for the task. They recognized that only God can truly see a person's inner character and fitness for spiritual work.

The disciples prayed for the chosen man to step into the apostolic ministry that Judas had abandoned. Judas had turned away to go to his own place, which refers to the punishment he deserved for his sins. This prayer shows that leadership in Christ's church is a sacred trust from God.

The believers cast lots to determine the outcome, following an Old Testament practice that entrusted the final choice to God's providence. The lot fell on Matthias, and he was officially added to the eleven apostles. This restored the symbolic number of twelve apostles just before the arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

differ.view: The disciples acted prematurely in casting lots, because God intended Paul to be the true replacement for Judas.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The election of Matthias is the first biblical example of apostolic succession, where the apostles fill a vacancy in their governing office.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars consider the account of choosing an apostle by lots to be a later, unhistorical tradition.
